Compress Images to 100 KB or 200 KB: Upload Guide

Fit a photo under an upload limit, keep required pixel dimensions and check the real output size before submitting.

Compress image to KB ↗Image resizer ↗Image compressor ↗
Common upload limits used by this tool
TargetMaximum bytesWhat to check
100 KB102,400File format and required pixel dimensions
200 KB204,800Whether the portal uses decimal KB instead
500 KB512,000The actual downloaded file size

Start with the complete upload rules

Write down the accepted format, maximum file size and required width and height. A 100 KB cap and a 600 × 600 pixel requirement are separate tests. The file can meet one and fail the other. If a portal requires JPEG, choose JPEG even if a WebP export would be smaller. Keep the original image while you prepare a copy.

Compress while keeping the original dimensions

Open Compress image to KB and choose your JPG, PNG or WebP source. Select an accepted output format and enter 100, 200 or another limit. Leave Allow smaller pixel dimensions unchecked when the original dimensions must stay fixed. Press Compress to target. The tool searches lower quality settings and offers a download only when the encoded file fits its byte limit.

Understand what keeping dimensions means

A 1600 × 900 image can remain 1600 × 900 while the saved file gets smaller. That does not mean its detail is unchanged. Lower JPEG or WebP quality can introduce soft edges and visible artifacts. Read the output dimensions and size, then inspect the downloaded image. The same quality setting produces different file sizes for different images.

If the target cannot be reached

First check whether the destination permits a different format. If it permits fewer pixels, resize the image proportionally or enable smaller dimensions and try again. If it requires fixed pixels, do not reduce them just to pass the byte limit. A very detailed image and a very small cap may be incompatible at acceptable quality. Toolnest reports when it cannot fit the target instead of offering a file that exceeds it.

Check bytes, not just the rounded KB label

Toolnest uses 1 KB = 1,024 bytes, so 100 KB means 102,400 bytes. A destination may instead enforce 100,000 bytes or display a rounded value. For a strict 100,000-byte cap, a target of 97 KB means at most 99,328 bytes in this tool. Check the downloaded file properties and the destination’s actual rule rather than relying on the rounded size alone.

Choose the next tool for the remaining problem

If only the pixel dimensions are wrong, use Image resizer with the aspect ratio locked. If only the format is wrong, use Image converter to create a real JPEG, PNG or WebP file. Renaming an extension does not change its encoding. Do not repeatedly recompress an already degraded copy; return to the original when possible.

Common questions

Can I compress to 100 KB without resizing?

Leave Allow smaller pixel dimensions unchecked. The tool will try lower JPEG or WebP quality at the original width and height. It may be impossible to meet a small limit with those dimensions; no oversized download is offered.

Does a smaller file mean no quality loss?

No. JPEG and lossy WebP compression can discard detail. Keeping the same pixel dimensions does not guarantee the same visual quality. Compare faces, edges and small text before using the download.

Why is a file below 100 KB still rejected?

Check its actual bytes, file format, dimensions and any other upload rules. Some portals use 100,000 bytes for 100 KB. Choose a lower target if necessary; meeting a size limit alone does not guarantee acceptance.
